parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by a scalar quantity and by a vector quantity.

markscheme_points.text: a vector has magnitude and direction

hints: Hint 1: Think about what information you need to fully describe a measurement - is just a number with a unit enough, or do you also need to say which way it acts?
Hint 2: Compare a quantity like temperature with a quantity like velocity to see the difference between magnitude only and magnitude plus direction.
parts.proper_answer: scalar: quantity with magnitude only. vector: quantity with magnitude and direction.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a Scalar Means**
Think of sitting beside me and I tell you the temperature is $20^{\circ}\text{C}$. You know everything you need. A scalar is complete once you give its size, called its magnitude, with its unit. No direction makes sense for it.

Step 2: **What a Vector Means**
Now if I tell you the velocity is $95\text{ m s}^{-1}$, you would ask - which way? A vector needs both pieces: how big it is, its magnitude, and which way it points, its direction. Velocity, force, momentum and displacement are all vectors.

parts.label: (b)

markscheme_points.text: power: scalar temperature: scalar momentum: vector
markscheme_points.guidance: (two correct 1 mark, all three correct 2 marks)

hints: Hint 1: Ask yourself for each quantity whether saying north, south, east or west adds any meaning to its value.
Hint 2: Recall that momentum involves velocity, $p = mv$, while power involves only energy transferred per unit time and temperature involves only hotness.
parts.proper_answer: power: scalar, temperature: scalar, momentum: vector.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Test For Direction**
A quick test is to ask if direction matters. Power is rate of energy transfer in $\text{W}$. $100\text{ W}$ north means nothing extra. Temperature is just how hot something is. Neither has a direction, so both are scalars.

Step 2: **Spot the Vector**
Momentum is mass times velocity, $$p = mv$$ Since velocity is a vector with direction, momentum inherits that direction. A momentum of $10\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ to the west is different from $10\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ to the east, so momentum is a vector.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
An aircraft is travelling in wind. Fig. 1.2 shows the velocities for the aircraft in still air and for the wind.
{{figure:figure_1_2}}
Fig. 1.2
The velocity of the aircraft in still air is $95\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to the west.
The velocity of the wind is $28\text{ m s}^{-1}$ from $65^{\circ}$ south of east.
parts.text: On Fig. 1.2, draw an arrow, labelled $R$, in the direction of the resultant velocity of the aircraft.

markscheme_points.text: arrow labelled R in a direction from 5° to 20° north of

hints: Hint 1: Imagine placing the tail of the wind arrow at the tip of the aircraft arrow - the resultant runs from the start to the finish and the small northward push will tilt it slightly north of west.
parts.proper_answer: Draw arrow labelled R starting at the junction, pointing to the west and slightly north of west, about 5 to 20 degrees north of west.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Visualising the Resultant**
You have a large $95\text{ m s}^{-1}$ arrow to the west and a smaller $28\text{ m s}^{-1}$ arrow pushing up and west. Add them tip-to-tail. The combined effect is still mainly west but lifted a little to the north. Draw that new arrow from the junction, pointing west-northwest, and label it $R$.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the magnitude of the resultant velocity of the aircraft.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the vector triangle - the two known sides are $95\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $28\text{ m s}^{-1}$ with an enclosed angle of $115^{\circ}$ when placed tip-to-tail.
Hint 2: Use the cosine rule for the magnitude, or resolve each velocity into west and north components and then combine with Pythagoras.
parts.proper_answer: $v \approx 1.1 \times 10^{2}\text{ m s}^{-1}$ (about $110\text{ m s}^{-1}$) to the west-northwest.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Setting Up the Cosine Rule**
Because the angle between the vectors in the triangle is not $90^{\circ}$, Pythagoras alone will not work. When the $28\text{ m s}^{-1}$ wind vector is added to the $95\text{ m s}^{-1}$ aircraft vector, the angle opposite the resultant is $115^{\circ}$. The cosine rule gives: $$V^{2} = 95^{2} + 28^{2} - 2 \times 95 \times 28 \times \cos 115^{\circ}$$

Step 2: **Calculating the Magnitude**
Evaluate carefully: $$V^{2} = 9025 + 784 - 5320 \times \cos 115^{\circ}$$ Since $\cos 115^{\circ}$ is negative, the last term adds. This gives $V^{2} \approx 12057$, so $$V = \sqrt{12057} \approx 110\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ Keep 2 or 3 significant figures with unit $\text{m s}^{-1}$. The wind speeds the aircraft up slightly in magnitude and pushes it north of west.
